clue.text: Did boar, having lost tail, moan sadly — being this?

definitions.note: The definition is a pointer rather than a synonym: 'this' sends you back to the state the rest of the clue describes.

indicators.note: A word's tail is its last letter, and a creature that has lost it hands over everything except that letter.
Something done sadly is done badly, and letters set down badly will not keep the order they were given in.

parts.note: the auxiliary verb taken at face value, three letters of fodder
the wild pig loses the R at its tail end, leaving three letters of fodder
four more letters of fodder, handed over whole

explanation.walkthrough: The clue defines itself: 'being this' points back at the picture the other words draw, a boar minus its tail, moaning. Everyman hides the deletion inside that picture by giving the animal a tail to lose.
explanation.definitionFit: A creature grumbling and short of its tail is out of sorts, and the phrase names exactly that temper, so the clue's own scene is the definition.

clue.text: In that case, reject outsiders for life with offspring, briefly

indicators.note: Outsiders are the letters standing at each end, and rejecting them leaves only what was in the middle.
A word said briefly is cut short, so the last letter of the one named is never written down.

parts.note: the two letters left when the L and the E at either end go
a son is offspring, docked of its final letter

explanation.walkthrough: Two small words, two separate trims, which is why a (2,2) can cost more thought than a long entry. 'Outsiders' means the outer letters, not people, and that reading is the whole of the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: 'If so' makes whatever follows conditional on what was just said, which is the job 'in that case' does in a sentence.

clue.text: Oh dear, a maiden scratching bottom

indicators.note: To scratch an entry is to strike it out, and in a down clue the bottom is the letter at the foot of the word.

parts.note: the indefinite article, taken as the single letter it is
lass is the northern word for a young unmarried woman, and her final letter is then struck out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching' does a nice double-take, rude on the surface and 'delete' underneath. Note also that 'maiden' is not the cricketing M here, which is the abbreviation the word usually signals.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the old written exclamation of regret, still printed where speech would say 'oh dear' — the same sigh in literary dress.

clue.text: Right to steal

definitions.meaning: fitting, suitable, the proper thing for the occasion
to take something over for your own use without asking, the sense in which land or funds get taken

explanation.walkthrough: Three words in all, and the trap is reading them as one phrase about entitlement. The stress moves between the two senses: the adjective is APP-ro-pri-'t, the verb app-ro-pri-ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both the adjective meaning fitting for the occasion and the verb meaning to take something over for yourself, which is a polite word for stealing.

clue.text: 1,002 buns going off in little roadster

indicators.note: Food that has gone off has turned, and letters that have turned will not stay in the order they were handed over.

parts.note: Roman numerals: M is a thousand and II is two
four more letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Little roadster' reads as a sports car and is the definition, not a piece of wordplay. The number is the way in: a comma in the middle of it is the setter making it look like an amount rather than four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadster in the older, wider sense is anything made to travel roads, so a small road vehicle answers it — not just an open two-seater.

clue.text: Primarily outrageous — beyond saucy — causing extremely nauseous emotions?

definitions.text: Primarily outrageous — beyond saucy — causing extremely nauseous emotions?

indicators.note: In the first place is what the word means, so it asks for each following word's opening letter and not the word itself.

parts.note: the opening letters of those three words, taken in order
four more openings, one from each of the remaining words

explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: the sentence is the wordplay and the definition at once. 'Primarily' works twice over, meaning 'chiefly' as you read it and 'take the first letters' as you solve it.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight through, the whole sentence describes something outrageous, past merely saucy and sickening to meet, which is what the word means.

clue.text: Copied sample from tape deck

indicators.note: A sample is a small piece cut out of something bigger, so the letters wanted run unbroken inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the run starts one letter into the first word and stops one letter into the second

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers like to straddle a join between words, because that is where the eye stops looking. The surface's recording gear has nothing to do with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to imitate them move for move, named after the animal, so the past tense matches 'copied' exactly.

clue.text: Tormented, so purified faithless

indicators.note: Something tormented has been twisted about and pulled out of shape, which is what happens here to the letters beside the word.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, exactly the length of the entry

explanation.walkthrough: The surface builds one religious picture — suffering that cleanses — out of an instruction and its letters. The definition then swings the sense round to treachery.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfidious means treacherous, breaking faith with someone who trusted you, so 'faithless' is the exact sense rather than the irreligious one.

clue.text: Senators regularly mugged off firebrands

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off has turned, and turned letters no longer sit in the order the clue printed them.
Something done regularly happens at fixed intervals, so letters are taken at every second place in the word rather than from all of them.

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the word, the odd ones left behind
six more letters of fodder, handed over whole

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mugged off' reads as one piece of modern slang, being made a fool of, and is two instructions underneath — the letters, then what to do with them.
explanation.definitionFit: A demagogue works a crowd up with fear and flattery, so 'firebrands' names them as rabble-rousers rather than as anything to do with fire.

clue.text: Quality in which you're quick — to anger?

definitions.text: Quality in which you're quick — to anger?

parts.note: read this far and it sounds like praise: briskness, a lively turn of speed
the dash makes you go back and re-read, and the quickness turns out to be a short temper

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the hinge of the clue. No letters are on offer anywhere, so the solve is spotting that one word carries both a compliment and an insult, and that the second one is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappiness is the quality of being snappy, and snappy covers both brisk and short-tempered; the question mark asks for the biting sense.

clue.text: Flipping Frenchman to get stuffed

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the letters named next are read the other way about — and across the grid that means right to left.

parts.note: Marc is an everyday French first name, the French spelling of Mark

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' passes as a mild oath in the surface, which is how the instruction hides in plain sight. Everyman clues Frenchmen by first name often enough to be worth expecting.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack something full — food into a mouth, people into a carriage — is what the answer means, and 'get stuffed' is the everyday way of saying it.

clue.text: Activity for four using Gregorian and Julian calendars?

definitions.meaning: two couples out together on the same evening, each pair keeping the other company
Britain swapped calendars in 1752, and for years afterwards a document carried both the Old Style and the New Style year

explanation.walkthrough: The 'four' is the giveaway that a social sense is wanted first, and the italics on 'and' insist both calendars are in play at once rather than one replacing the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The social sense is two couples on one outing; the historical sense is marking a document with both the old and the new year at once.

clue.text: Hands up — then they may give you the lot

definitions.text: Hands up — then they may give you the lot

parts.note: on the surface a stick-up; in a saleroom a raised hand is a bid

parts.words: then they may give you the lot
parts.note: 'the lot' shifts from everything you own to the numbered item under the hammer

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the sentence swap meaning together, which is why nothing can be split off as wordplay: the robbery reading and the saleroom reading use exactly the same words.
explanation.definitionFit: An auctioneer takes bids from raised hands and knocks each lot down to whoever bids highest, so the whole sentence is a description of the job.

clue.text: Lack of liveliness — but stable, Spooner says

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for trading the opening sounds of two words as he spoke, so naming him is the whole instruction.

parts.note: a stable is where nags are kept, so it can be read as a station for nags
trade the openings of those two words, N for ST, and say the result aloud

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' is the trap: it wants to mean steady, and the reverend needs the building full of horses instead. Spoonerisms are easiest worked from the definition end, then sounded backwards to check.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnation is what sets in when nothing moves or grows — water, an economy, a career — which is a lack of liveliness in one word.

clue.text: Corporate staple: member of global minority on committee

indicators.note: In a down entry a thing sitting on another is written above it, so the piece named first ends up at the top.

parts.note: counted worldwide rather than nationally, white people are in the minority
the board of a company is its governing committee

explanation.walkthrough: 'Global' is the word that makes the first piece fair, and it is easy to skim past: the minority is a minority of the planet, not of the office. The colon does the work of an equals sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Every meeting room has one on the wall with a marker beside it, so 'corporate staple' points at it as standard office equipment.

clue.text: Clobber boisterous marsh tits, not keeping mum

indicators.note: A boisterous crowd will neither stand still nor stay in line, and the letters beside the word behave the same way.
What is not kept is let go, so the two letters named next are dropped before anything else happens.

parts.note: ma is the nursery word for mother, and these are the two letters taken out
the marsh tit is a small British woodland bird; its nine letters lose that pair before the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks exactly like the anagram signal — to clobber is to hit — and it is the definition instead: British slang for clothes or gear. 'Keeping mum' is a second red herring, staying silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Clobber is British slang for clothes and kit generally, so the plural garment sits inside it as one of the things you turn up wearing.

clue.text: Runs off, about to throw up artwork

definitions.note: The answer wears an -ing ending but is a noun like the definition: it names the finished print, not the act of making one.

indicators.note: Taking something off is removing it, so the letter named just before this word is stripped from the front of what follows.

parts.note: to retch is to heave as though vomiting were a moment away
R is the cricket scoreboard's abbreviation for runs, and it is this letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw up' tempts you towards a reversal, and this is an across entry where nothing goes up at all. 'Runs off' is a second trap: one phrase on the surface, two separate instructions underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: An etching is a print pulled from a plate the artist has bitten with acid, so it is artwork in the plainest sense of a work of art.

clue.text: Arrive home and recover

definitions.meaning: to return to where you started, at the end of a journey
to have something lost returned to you — a wallet, a deposit, a borrowed book

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same phrasal verb, which is why 'and' is all the join needed. In the first you are the thing that moves; in the second something moves back to you.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both to return to where you set out from and to have a lost thing returned, as in getting your money back.

clue.text: Chess pieces: more than one black, you say?

indicators.note: Saying a word puts its sound in play rather than its spelling, so what is wanted is another way of writing the same noise.

parts.note: night is when the sky is black, and 'more than one' makes it plural; that plural sounds identical to a word that starts with a silent letter

explanation.walkthrough: The colon separates definition from wordplay. The joke is entirely in the spelling: one word begins with a letter nobody pronounces, so the two are impossible to tell apart out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: The knight is the chess piece carved as a horse's head that jumps in an L, so 'chess pieces' names the plural precisely.

clue.text: The French certain — this writer's assumed — to be working? Not so

definitions.note: The definition arrives as a negated verb phrase — 'not working' — while the answer is the noun for that state, so it describes rather than substitutes.

indicators.note: To assume something is to take it in and absorb it, so the letter named here is taken inside the other pieces rather than added at the end.

parts.note: the masculine form of 'the' in French
the setter referring to himself, which in crosswords is one letter
certain of something is sure of it, the plain synonym

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue and works by negation: the question mark and 'not so' turn 'working' inside out before you may use it.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is the time left over when work is not being done, so a phrase saying you are not at work lands on it exactly.

clue.text: Characters implicated in doleful 'Et tu' — centurion leaves

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer is a mass noun for the whole head, so the setter is naming the parts and asking for the thing they make up.

indicators.note: Characters are letters, and something implicated in a thing is caught up inside it, so the run sits unbroken within the words that follow.

parts.note: the run begins at the end of the first word and stops two letters into the last, straight through the quoted Latin

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' wants to be the verb of the surface, the centurion walking out, and it is the definition — the salad kind. Caesar's dying words are there to make the span look like a quotation rather than a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A lettuce is grown and eaten as a head of leaves, so 'leaves' names it by the only part of it anyone puts on a plate.

clue.text: Striking bargain — six slices of butter — alternately shortening

indicators.note: A bargain that is struck has been hit, and letters that take a knock do not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, handed over whole
six written in Roman numerals

indicators.note: Alternately means every other one, so only every second letter of the word beside it is picked up.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the dairy word, the rest left on the plate

explanation.walkthrough: Butter and shortening belong to one baking picture, and that is the misdirection: the definition is the other sense of shortening, cutting a word down to a few letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To abbreviate is to cut a word or phrase down to something briefer, so 'shortening' is the plain synonym in the matching -ing form.

clue.text: Arm or leg displaying scale (not the first)

indicators.note: The bracket excuses one letter from duty, and the one excused is the letter the word starts with.

parts.note: to scale a wall or a peak is to climb it, the verb rather than the noun

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scale' is the trap, because the fish's and the map's are the first senses that arrive and the clue wants the verb. In a four-letter entry that one substitution is most of the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Arms and legs are two of the things the word covers, along with wings and branches, so the definition works by naming examples of the category.

clue.text: King once called: Attack!

parts.note: K is the king on a chessboard and in a pack of cards
nee is the French for 'born', used in English before the name a married woman was known by earlier

explanation.walkthrough: The colon is doing the work of an equals sign. The exclamation mark sells the definition as a shout of command, which disguises the fact that it is a verb rather than a battle cry.
explanation.definitionFit: To knee someone is to drive that joint into them, a street-fighter's move, so the verb answers an order to attack.

clue.text: Och! Hebridean island's loch has vanished!

indicators.note: Something that has vanished is simply gone, so the letter named just before it is nowhere in what remains.

parts.note: Islay is one of the larger islands of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland, famous for its whiskies
maps shorten a Scottish loch to L, and that is the letter dropped here

explanation.walkthrough: Everything in the surface is Scottish — the exclamation, the island, the water — so the letter that goes missing is the Scottish one too. The definition is the English equivalent of that opening noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of surprise or mild protest, one Scots and one clubbable English, and either can stand alone as a whole utterance.

clue.text: Geoffrey's repaired cane chair, you said?

definitions.note: The clue names the man by his first name in the possessive, while the answer is the adjective built from his surname.

indicators.note: A chair that has been repaired has been taken apart and put together differently, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, one short of the entry

indicators.note: Saying a word asks for its sound and not its spelling, so the pronoun arrives as the single letter it sounds like.

parts.note: the pronoun said aloud is the name of a letter, which supplies the tenth

explanation.walkthrough: The first name alone is fair in a Sunday puzzle: only one Geoffrey has an adjective named after him. 'You said' is the neat touch, sounding a single letter into the fodder rather than sounding the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucerian means belonging to or in the style of Geoffrey Chaucer, poet of the Canterbury Tales, so the first name points at the man behind the adjective.

clue.text: Gesture of agreement: Everyman's beginning to be a knob

parts.note: the dip of the head that says yes without speaking

indicators.note: A word's beginning is the letter it starts with, so only that one letter comes from the name in front of it.

parts.note: the first letter of the setter's own pen name, which he uses as a piece of wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his clues: the setter's pseudonym is fodder here, a habit worth expecting each week. The colon again stands in for an equals sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a knob or swelling where something joins or thickens, the sense that survives in nodule and in the lymph nodes a doctor feels for.

clue.text: See in blots — splotchy — what's apparent

indicators.note: Blots that run into one another keep no clean shape, and neither does the order of the letters beside the word.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder: the verb, the preposition and the stains, all taken at face value

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an inkblot test, where seeing something in the blots is the whole point. 'See' and 'in' look like instructions and are letters, which is the usual trap in a long anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostensible describes what a thing appears to be on the surface as against what it really is, so 'apparent' is the exact sense, not merely the obvious one.
